title: Design: Move audit logs to object storage

defects.correction: Amazon S3 is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability; 99.99% is the availability design target of the S3 Standard storage class.
defects.note: [multi-part] [secondary-source] The launch year (2006) is right; only the durability figure is wrong, and it is easily confused with the availability figure. The primary source is the AWS S3 documentation.

defects.quote: S3 is only eventually consistent, so a read that follows a write may return stale data.
defects.correction: Since December 2020, Amazon S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency for all requests.
defects.note: [secondary-source] Older blog posts and answers that describe eventual consistency still rank highly; the primary sources are the AWS announcement of December 2020 and the current S3 documentation.

defects.quote: Moving the logs will reduce storage costs by 90%.
Auditors have never asked us for logs older than a year, so we can delete everything after twelve months.
defects.known_rebuttal: What auditors happened to ask for in the past is not the retention requirement. Retention is set by law, contract and standards: many financial and regulatory regimes require records to be kept for six or seven years, security standards such as PCI DSS set minimum periods of their own, and a litigation hold can require logs to be preserved indefinitely. Breaches are often discovered long after they begin, so old logs are exactly what an investigation needs. Deletion cannot be undone, while cold object storage costs very little, so the period should come from a written retention policy.
